I played "Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You" through in about 4 hours. Surely, it was somewhat entertaining, but I do think I should've gotten more out of it for the money. Having said that, I don't think it's impossible that I would ever replay it, considering the story can change depending on your actions. 

What I found interesting about the game was that I kept feeling that I was the main enemy - and yet I found myself enjoying the power I held. Psychologically, it was a different experience. I am happy with the ending I got. 

The main issue I had with the game was how limited I felt throughout it. Basically - you play as an investigator and loads up information to a network made to, well, spy on people. However, what information you can load up is already pre-decided by the game, which at times left the player with knowledge that couldn't be used in game. In addition, you couldn't take any data back or update it - unless the game wanted you to. The Orwell-system in the game didn't feel fully developed.

In conclusion, I feel as if the game was released before it was fully finished. I often felt frustrated, wondering why I wasn't able to upload information I found interesting, and that it felt unrealistic that such a complex system wouldn't be able to handle conflicting data. But I did find the concept interesting.

I wish there was a "Maybe" rating. This was so solidly middle of the road. A Perfect 2.5/5. This game is a narrative uncovered through a government surveillance system, and we're really taking the good with the bad here. 

The good: The mechanics of the game are interesting, and pay off in a very satisfying way. The visuals are nice and the interface is inoffensive. 

The bad: The character writing is mealymouthed, badly-paced and lacking a fresh core message. The narrative is hung on characters that are one-dimensional. The message is nothing new, but the 1984 But It's Got Facebook appeal could sell it's rhetorical points a lot easier if these characters felt rounder or even spoke in a slightly modern voice. A game where you follow people's daily communications should lead to these characters feeling richer and more developed. But it managed to avoid that altogether in favor of long, trite conversations, and worldbuilding with zero payoff. There were also a few shaky attempts at social commentary? For a game about investigating people for voicing their Alternative Ideologies, it all felt flimsy, like it didn't have enough confidence to have a real point of view. To it's credit, the story itself had some really interesting and surprising turns! But it was all at the end, AND all at once in a truly maddening choice of pacing.

All this is... fine, I suppose, considering these characters' actions and moral codas don't feel meaningfully attached to the larger ethical decision you're ultimately faced with. Instead, I felt like I was reading a 90's screenplay about Post-college Anarchist Mallrats and their One Cool Professor trying to make their mark on the world. Mostly because Orwell takes itself really, painfully seriously.

Overall, worth playing for the moments where the story and gameplay align nicely, but DEFINITELY get it on sale. Full price? Idk. Torrent Hackers instead. It has the same self-important tone and fakey computer-whiz stuff, but at least that had Angelina Jolie in it.

The story is short, but I found myself interested in reaching the end the entire time. I felt dirty and invasive, combing through people's lives in an attempt to ...spoilers. The plot is such: there is a threat to security and it is your job to find out who perpetrated the action and to stop them. You comb through newspapers and social media to discover links between people and actions. You listen in on their phone calls and you read their texts/emails to catch them using the wrong words. Just like people though, there are lies being told between people and it's your job to clean up any existing data conflicts. Now that I know the story, I'm unsure of replayability at this time. The first go through was completely worth it for an afternoon of fun. Unless there is something I'm missing, I concluded my investigation in just over 3 hours. Honestly my biggest complaint was the speed at which the people texted or spoke on the phone. I found it to be slow. You can change the speed of these messages though in the settings. I would caution against changing this too much though. Towards the end of the game, the speed is a bit too quick to keep up. I did not like this as it felt like rushing through conversations and I was unable to peruse at my own pace.

I do recommend this game, but really only if it's on sale. It is quite short. 

Overall I give this a 9.2/10. I will most likely be playing it again, especially to see about getting the rest of the achievements.

This is one of the more unique games I've played.  If the themes of George Orwell's 1984 resonate with you (and they might, regardless of whether you know that famous work or not--the concept of "Big Brother" is pretty much in the cultural lexicon, regardless of familiarity with its origin), then this will definitely interest you.  If you like detective games, it scratches that itch as well.  There's a good amount of interactivity, even though the game is primarily story-driven.  The act of what is essentially data-mining is nicely streamlined so that it isn't really too tedious.  When new "datachunks" are revealed, it really feels like relevant discovery, slowly building a picture from tiny puzzle pieces of data.  There's some choice in the game, as well, though not so much that repeated playthroughs would result in a lot of variation.  However, at 4 hours, I've played through the game once, so it isn't a vast time investment.  At $2.49, due to the Steam summer sale, the price was such that even a disappointment wouldn't have bothered me much.  But I was pleasantly surprised.  I'm going to play the second one as well.  Snatch this up when on sale.  I don't think you'll be too disappointed either.

I mean I do get the message when I see those personal information and communication spied on, lives of actual people disturbed and destroyed, and involuntarily think of Orwell now whenever I type a private message on my device. But these are spontaneous "feelings" I get from the game, which is good, but not "lessons" that Juliet could make me learn in the few threatening sentences.
